messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

in the usual definition of the cumulative family, the probability for category k is given by

F(Intercept[k+1] - eta) - F(Intercept[k] - eta)

where F is a cumulative distribution function (the logistic distribution using the logit link),
and eta contain all fixed and random effects predictor terms except for the fixed effects intercepts (also called thresholds in ordinal models).

This formulation ensures that positive regression coefficients imply higher prob. for higher categories when the value of the predictor is larger.

Howver, in this notation, we have to compute fixed - random effects intercepts to get to the intercepts for each group, since the random intercepts
are part or eta.

With respect to the priors: Yes they seem ok, although I would except the model to run well without specifying them.

One question though: For what reason did you add weights to your model?

Hi,

I am getting some unexpected results using a varying intercept model with population level predictors.

I would like to get `fitted` results for a new cluster or level in my model. In particular, I would like the new intercept to be sampled from a normal distribution with mean equal to zero and standard deviation `sd(Intercept)` found from the model.

Based on the documentation, it sounded like I need to set `allow_new_levels = TRUE` and `sample_new_levels = 'gaussian'`. However, I am getting an error.

As shown in my working example below, other values such as `sample_new_levels='uncertainty'` or `'old_levels'` work.  Fitted also works when `re_formula = NA`, but I am almost certain (based on my reconstruction of the link function) that is not what I want.

Any ideas?

Thanks,

Tim

library(brms)
library(rethinking)

data("chimpanzees")
d <- chimpanzees
d$recipient <- NULL

mod <- brm( pulled_left ~ 1 + (1 | actor) +
              prosoc_left*condition - condition,
            data = d, family = bernoulli(), iter = 5000,
            prior = c(set_prior("normal(0,10)", class = 'Intercept'),
                      set_prior("normal(0,10)", class = 'b'),
                      set_prior("cauchy(0,1)", class = 'sd',
                                group = 'actor')))

d.pred <- data.frame(prosoc_left = c(0,1,0,1),
           condition = c(0,0,1,1),
           actor = c(8,8,8,8))

# doesn't work

       sample_new_levels = "gaussian")

  # Error in cor[, k] : subscript out of bounds
  # In addition: Warning messages:
  # 1: In min(cor) : no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf
  # 2: In max(cor) : no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf

> Hi Paul,
>
> in the usual definition of the cumulative family, the probability for category k is given by
>
> F(Intercept[k+1] - eta) - F(Intercept[k] - eta)
>
> where F is a cumulative distribution function (the logistic distribution using the logit link),
> and eta contain all fixed and random effects predictor terms except for the fixed effects intercepts (also called thresholds in ordinal models).
>
> This formulation ensures that positive regression coefficients imply higher prob. for higher categories when the value of the predictor is larger.
>
> Howver, in this notation, we have to compute fixed - random effects intercepts to get to the intercepts for each group, since the random intercepts
> are part or eta.
>
> With respect to the priors: Yes they seem ok, although I would except the model to run well without specifying them.
>
> One question though: For what reason did you add weights to your model?

messages.subject_clean: Controlling orders of monotonic predictors in multivariate regression
messages.body_plain:
I'm working on a multivariate model with monotonic predictors. If I were to code this with brms, my formula would look something like:

brms::bf(cbind(y1, y2) ~ mo(Condition))

As I understand it, that formula implies that the effect of Condition on y1 and y2 will be forced to have the same order (1 < 2 < 3 < 4, for both y1 and y2). Is there a way to control the ordering of the effect of Condition on each of the outcomes separately? That is, would there be a way to specify that the effect of Condition on y1 followed 1 < 2 < 3 < 4, but the effect on y2 followed 1 < 3 < 2 < 4?

Thanks for your time,
Patrick

messages.subject: Give prior probability to mixing proportions in brms mixture model
messages.subject_clean: Give prior probability to mixing proportions in brms mixture model
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I'd like to use the mixture model feature in brms to model a mixture of two gaussians. I've followed the example from the brms manual and the model seems to converge and the diagnostics look fine. In order to take full advantage of the Bayesian approach, I'd like to set a prior for the mixing proportions of the two gaussians to express my belief whats the proportion of theta1 and theta2. The example shows how to predict the proportion as well as setting the proportions as fixed. My idea so far is to set a very narrow normal distribution as prior to b_theta2 to express my belief that the mixing proportion of theta is let's say around p=0.3. A quick test showed that setting the mean of the prior completely off (e.g. mean of 10) that the mixing becomes worse, which is the expected behaviour. But I'm not entirely sure if this is the way to go or if there is a better way to do it. E.g. directly setting the prior probability to .3. I think, I should probably also give a prior to the Intercept of theta2 in that case?! Do you have any suggestions on how to set a prior probability of the mixing proportions in a mixture model in brms? Ideally the mixing proportions would still be predicted by a variable (e.g. x), but using an informative prior to express my belief on the actual mixing proportion. Sorry if that makes no sense at all. Here's the tweaked example from the reference manual:

# simulate some data
set.seed(1234)
dat <- data.frame(
  y = c(rnorm(200), rnorm(100, 6)),
  x = rnorm(300),
  z = sample(0:1, 300, TRUE)
)

# fit a simple normal mixture model
mix <- mixture(gaussian, gaussian)
prior <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 7), Intercept, dpar = mu1),
  prior(normal(5, 7), Intercept, dpar = mu2),
  prior(normal(0.3,0.1), b, dpar= theta2)#, #prior for mixing proportions
  #prior(normal(10,0.1), b, dpar= theta2) #'wrong' prior for demonstration purposes
)

# predict the mixing proportions
fit4 <- brm(bf(y ~ x + z, theta2 ~ x),
            dat, family = mix, prior = prior,
            inits = 0, chains = 2)
summary(fit4)
pp_check(fit4)

Thanks for your help!

messages.subject: Forming a hypothesis with interactions
messages.body_plain:
How would I evaluate the hypothesis that a treatment is better than another treatment when there is an interaction?

For example, I was playing around with the sleepstudy example from lme4.

data(sleepstudy, package = "lme4")
library(dplyr)
library(brms)
options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

sleepstudy %>%
  filter(Subject %excluding% c(308, 351, 372, 371)) %>%
  mutate(treatment = as.factor(ifelse(row_number(Subject) < 91, "1", "2"))) -> ss2

m_slp_br <- brm(Reaction ~ Days * treatment + (Days |Subject),
                data = ss2,
                family = gaussian(),
                iter = 4000,
                control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9))

I know I can test the main effect simply with:

hypothesis(m_slp_br, "treatment2 < 0")

It tells me that the second level of treatment is probably worse than the first level.

But I also see that the interaction term is almost certainly positive:

hypothesis(m_slp_br, "Days:treatment2 > 0")

My guess is that to test this, I need:

hypothesis(m_slp_br, "treatment2 + Days:treatment2*5 < 0")

Which I think tells me that by day 5, there is a significant improvement with treatment2 vs treatment 1.

Am I interpreting that correctly?

mu[i] ~ non-linear function

Thanks,

1. The higher the ranefs, the higher the probabilities for higher categories.

You can think of the ranefs as being on the logit scale, although the situation in ordinal models in a bit more complicate than that.

2. You could use for instance

fitted(model, newdata = data.frame(B = unique(D$B)), re_formula = ~ (1|B))

to only include the random effects of B in the predictions (and not those of C).

3. brms assumes a normal distribution (normal prior) for the random effects, just as most other multilevel packages do.

Best,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've come across some differences between rstanarm and brms, that I'm not able to explain. I hope someone here can tell me why I'm seeing these behaviors. Below is a reproducible example:

library(languageR) #for data
library(rstanarm)
library(brms)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot)
library(tidyr)

stan.pen <- stan_lmer(RT ~ list*priming + (priming|subjects) + (1|items), data=splitplot,
                      prior=normal(0,250), prior_intercept=normal(500,200))
p <- c(set_prior('normal(0,250)', class='b'),
       set_prior('normal(500,200)', class='Intercept', coef=''))

brm.pen <- brm(RT ~ list*priming + (priming|subjects) + (1|items),
               data=splitplot, prior=p)

As far as I can tell, those two models should be the same, but they are apparently not.

newdat <- expand.grid(list = rownames(table(splitplot$list)),
                      priming = rownames(table(splitplot$priming)),
                      subjects='0',
                      items = rownames(table(splitplot$items)))

temp <- as.data.frame(
  rstanarm::posterior_linpred(stan.pen, re.form = NA,
                    newdata = newdat, allow_new_levels=T)) #the linear predictor
temp$sample <- seq(1, length(temp$`1`))
newdat$index <- as.character(seq(1, length(newdat$list)))

temp %>%
  gather(index, prediction, -sample) %>%
  left_join(newdat) %>%
  group_by(list, priming) %>%
  summarise(est = mean(prediction), #mean of the linear predictor
            lower = quantile(prediction, .025),
            upper = quantile(prediction, .975)) %>% #upper and lower 95% uncertainty intervals
  mutate(model='rstanarm') -> plot.dat

temp <- as.data.frame(
  brms::posterior_linpred(brm.pen, re.form = NA,
                              newdata = newdat, allow_new_levels=T)) #linear predictor
temp$sample <- seq(1, length(temp$`V1`))
newdat$index <- as.character(paste('V', seq(1, length(newdat$list)), sep=''))

temp %>%
  gather(index, prediction, -sample) %>%
  left_join(newdat) %>%
  group_by(list, priming) %>%
  summarise(est = mean(prediction), #mean of the linear predictor
            lower = quantile(prediction, .025),
            upper = quantile(prediction, .975)) %>% #upper and lower 95% uncertainty intervals
  mutate(model='brms') %>%
  rbind(plot.dat) -> plot.dat

ggplot(plot.dat, aes(x=list, y=est, group=model, color=model)) +
  geom_point(position=position_dodge(width=.5)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=lower, ymax=upper), position=position_dodge(width=.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~priming)

This produces the following figure:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-AGo041SIOMY/Wg5PVxxB6OI/AAAAAAAAJMA/dSdOcMaeTyMQhPnri97tf9flOgx1RKf3QCLcBGAs/s1600/eg_fig.jpeg>

So it seems the mean is correct, but the uncertainty intervals do not match. Why not?

I've looked at some of the actual parameters estimated, and I think there's some differences in the covariance matrix:

stan.df <- data.frame(stan.pen)
brm.df <- data.frame(brm.pen)

df <- data.frame(model = c(rep('rstanarm', 4000),
                           rep('brms', 4000)),

                 intercept = c(stan.df$X.Intercept., brm.df$b_Intercept),
                 b_listlistB = c(stan.df$listlistB, brm.df$b_listlistB),
                 b_primingunprimed = c(stan.df$primingunprimed,
                                       brm.df$b_primingunprimed),
                 b_list_priming = c(stan.df$listlistB.primingunprimed,
                                    brm.df$b_listlistB.primingunprimed),
                 sigma = c(stan.df$sigma, brm.df$sigma),
                 sigma.items_int = c(stan.df$Sigma.items..Intercept...Intercept..,
                                     brm.df$sd_items__Intercept),
                 sigma.subjects_int = c(stan.df$Sigma.subjects..Intercept...Intercept..,
                                        brm.df$sd_subjects__Intercept),
                 sigma.subjects_priming.int = c(stan.df$Sigma.subjects.primingunprimed..Intercept..,
                                                brm.df$cor_subjects__Intercept__primingunprimed),
                 sigma.subjects_priming = c(stan.df$Sigma.subjects.primingunprimed.primingunprimed.,
                                            brm.df$sd_subjects__primingunprimed))

df %>%
  gather(parameter, value, intercept:sigma.subjects_priming) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=value, group=model, color=model)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, scales='free')

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-zhmQ9kP8wX8/Wg5QqHBwvwI/AAAAAAAAJMM/yiHkh0abNNogME80wUB09vh22ldEI9DIQCLcBGAs/s1600/eg_fig2.jpeg>

Sorry if I've missed something obvious in the documentation. What explains this behavior? Even if I'm misunderstanding the parameters (or something), I would expect the function `posterior_linpred` to perform identically in these situations, unless I've misspecified the model...

Hi Paul,

The reason I am trying to do this in stan is that I am working on a multi-level spline model that I don't know how to set up in brms.

The simple version of the model is

y ~ s(x), family = "bernoulli"

which can be trivially implemented in brms, where x is the log ratio of relative abundances of some bacteria in human body. Those log ratios are measured with some measurement error. In practice, one samples each bacteria type in a given biological sample and the number of bacteria of all types in the i-th sample is n[i], the number of bacteria 1 is x1[i] and bacteria 2 in sample i is x2[i]. Thus, lp1[i] and lp2[i] are the ML estimate of relative abundances of bacteria 1 and 2 in the i-th sample. These ML estimates of log relative abundandes are assumed to come from a normal distribution centered at true log relative abundances tlp1[i] and tlp2[i] for bug 1and 2, respectively. Standard deviations, denoted above as sigma[i], depend on ML estimates and are passed to the model as data.

A spline model accounting for measurement errors has the following structure

 y ~ bernoulli_logit( mu );

for( i in 1:N )
{
    x1[i] ~ binomial(n[i], exp(lp1[i]));
    lp1[i] ~ normal(tlp1[i], sigma[i]);
    x2[i] ~ binomial(n[i], exp(lp2[i]));
    lp2[i] ~ normal(tlp2[i], sigma[i]);
}

x = tlp1 - tlp2;
mu = "spline expression for x"

Is there a way to set it up in brms?

Thanks !
:)
